title: Trump admin using AI to deny medical care for seniors in disastrous experiment
gist: CMS's WISeR pilot brings AI/ML-driven prior authorization to traditional Medicare in six states, paying private vendors (Innovaccer, Zyter, Virtix) 25% of benchmark costs 'averted' by denials, with only a 5-10% quality-score haircut for bad denials. EFF-obtained documents show a rushed, error-prone rollout with weeks-long delays and denial rates above 50% at one vendor, yet CMS plans to expand the model to oncology, imaging, cardiac devices and more through 2031 despite a GAO finding of improper procedure.

insights.claim: CMS's WISeR (Wasteful and Inappropriate Service Reduction) model introduced AI/ML-based prior authorization into traditional Medicare in January 2026 across six states (New Jersey, Ohio, Oklahoma, Texas, Arizona, Washington) and is slated to run through the end of 2031.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Traditional Medicare, historically free of prior auth, is becoming a multi-year addressable market for AI utilization-management vendors.

insights.claim: WISeR currently requires prior authorization for about a dozen services, including nerve stimulation, epidural steroid injections, cervical fusions, skin substitutes for wounds, and incontinence and impotence treatments.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Providers and device makers in pain management, spine and wound care face slower Medicare volume and cash flow in pilot states.

insights.claim: CMS documents show plans to expand WISeR prior authorization to cancer treatments, air ambulance transport, advanced imaging such as MRIs, cardiac catheterization, pacemakers, implantable cardioverter defibrillators, and genetic and molecular lab tests.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Expansion would put Medicare volumes for oncology, imaging, cardiac-device and molecular-diagnostics companies under prior-auth friction; watch for rollout timing.

insights.claim: WISeR vendors are paid 25% of the regional benchmark cost of each service they deny, a 'share of averted expenditures' payment model.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Vendor revenue scales directly with denial volume, making denial rate the key revenue driver for AI prior-auth contractors in this model.
insights.quote: novel payment approach where the model participants are compensated based on a share of averted expenditures

insights.claim: The CMS Office of the Actuary warned in a memo that WISeR's payment design gives participants an incentive to deny as many claims as possible.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The government's own actuaries flagged the misaligned incentive, strengthening the political and legal case against the model.
insights.quote: model participants will have an incentive to deny as many claims as possible.
insights.locator: Murray further quoted the CMS Office of the Actuary

insights.claim: WISeR's Aggregate Quality Score penalty for bad denials is small: vendors scoring 85-100% keep all of their 25% share, 60-84% keep 95% of it, and below 60% still keep 90%.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Even a failing vendor loses at most 10% of denial-based revenue, so the quality adjustment barely restrains aggressive denials.
insights.locator: But the CMS documents reveal that this adjustment

insights.claim: Vendors are not paid when a denial is appealed and overturned, but few denials are appealed: the article cites 11.5% of denials appealed, with 80% of appeals overturning the denial.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Low appeal rates mean most wrongful denials likely stay profitable for vendors; the high overturn rate points to a large volume of inappropriate denials.
insights.quote: only 11.5 percent of care denials are appealed—though 80 percent of appeals result in the denial being overturned
insights.locator: Companies won't be paid if an authorization denial

insights.claim: Chris Klomp, the CMS deputy administrator directing Medicare and nominee for HHS Deputy Secretary, told the Senate his understanding was that WISeR contractors do not make more money by denying care, which CMS's own documents contradict.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Leadership misstatements on the incentive design create confirmation and oversight risk for the program.

insights.claim: Innovaccer was so unprepared for WISeR that it asked CMS to delay the launch and, when refused, temporarily auto-approved all prior authorization requests.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Shows the AI prior-auth technology was not production-ready at launch, a reputational and execution risk for the vendors involved.
insights.quote: [A]uto-affirming is the only path available that avoids creating a backlog of unprocessed prior authorizations and claims
insights.locator: According to the documents released by the EFF

insights.claim: WISeR vendor Zyter had data discrepancies for months, apparently because it did not understand the difference between Medicare Part A and Part B; its CEO says it is now fully functional across both.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Basic domain errors at contracted vendors point to weak CMS vendor vetting in AI-driven government healthcare programs.
insights.locator: But others carried on. One vendor, Zyter

insights.claim: Innovaccer did not respond to Ars Technica but told Stat News its WISeR technology is now fully live, while Ohio providers reported being unable to reach a human at Innovaccer for weeks.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Provider-support failures are a reputational risk for Innovaccer in its government health business.
insights.quote: THERE IS NO WAY TO GET A HOLD OF A HUMAN TO TALK TO

insights.claim: As of a March 30 weekly report, WISeR vendor Virtix had reviewed 6,096 prior authorization requests, approving 2,863 and denying 3,233 (53%).
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: A majority-denial rate under a paid-per-denial model is the key evidence critics use against WISeR and similar AI utilization management.

insights.claim: WISeR targets prior authorization decisions within 72 hours, but many took weeks or months, with at least one request still pending after 83 days.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Delays shift or cut procedure volumes for providers in pilot states and strengthen the political case to curb the program.
insights.quote: had a surgery pushed back almost two months due to zero communication.
insights.locator: In addition to a questionable number of denials

insights.claim: CMS put Virtix on a Corrective Action Plan for missing the 72-hour window; Virtix says the plan ended August 14 and its average turnaround is now 1.18 days for prior authorization and 1.17 days for prepayment review.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: CMS is enforcing timeliness but not denial rates; vendor-reported improvements are unverified by CMS in the article.
insights.locator: It was revealed in June that Virtix

insights.claim: Virtix argues WISeR denials rest on CMS's existing National and Local Coverage Determinations rather than vendor-set criteria, shifting responsibility for denials onto CMS policy.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: Vendors' defense is that they only apply CMS rules, which could limit their liability exposure if the program is challenged.

insights.claim: The Government Accountability Office found in May that the Trump administration did not follow proper procedure in setting up WISeR, calling its legality into question, yet the program continues with expansion plans.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: An open legality question is a tail risk for WISeR contracts and vendor revenue if challenged in court or Congress.

insights.claim: Democrats, including Rep. Suzan DelBene and Sen. Patty Murray, are pushing to expose and stop WISeR, but House Republicans voted down a committee effort to force release of more program documents.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: With party-line support holding, WISeR likely continues near term; its durability depends on political control rather than performance data.
insights.quote: I am going to do everything I can to stop this. It is really hurting patients.

insights.claim: Critics frame WISeR as a step toward privatizing traditional Medicare by handing care-approval decisions to private contractors.
insights.speaker: Beth Mole
insights.so_what: The privatization framing makes WISeR a likely campaign issue, raising headline risk for firms selling AI utilization management to government payers.
